utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I just have two brief points before the cross-examination begins. The first point, based on something that was raised by the accused at the end of yesterday's session, I checked on what was Prosecution's Exhibit 245, and the original document that was in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor, the instructions that are part of that exhibit are 13 pages. In other words, we only have the first 13 pages. That is simply all that we have of that document. The second point I would just like to bring to the Court's attention is that I have a long-standing medical appointment later this morning, so I will probably stand up and leave the courtroom at about 10.00, and if there is any re-examination of this witness, Mr. Ryneveld will take control of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true that from your superiors, on the eve of the NATO bombing, you asked to take the first part of your holiday, to go off on holiday on the 24th of March, 1999? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went on sick leave in February. I was using sick leave, and I didn't return to my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the members of the KLA, did they threaten you and say that unless you left the administration for the defence of Pristina that they would kidnap your son Visar, and that they intercepted and threatened your daughters Shpresa, Violeta and Goda, and did you suffer from these threats? Did they threaten you, in fact?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are lies on your part, and you're trying to manipulate things. Nobody was scared of the KLA in Kosova. It was a glorious army that fought for the rights of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Aliu, I know it's difficult being cross-examined, but we don't want, I'm afraid, speeches. We just want an answer. If it's not true, just say no. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what's the next question? Next question. No. We will go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that your request to use your holiday you explained by saying that you had been threatened by members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is this true: That when you went on holiday because of all the pressure exerted upon you and all the explanations that you gave, that you cried in front of your friends and comrades?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, you mustn't misrepresent what the witness said. He didn't say he went on holiday, he said he took sick leave. But go on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Take a look at this decision of the Federal Ministry for Defence in which we can see that on the basis of the rules and regulations to which this decision refers, Aliu Shukri, an employee of the Federal Ministry for Defence of the Republic of Serbia, the administration for the defence of Pristina, terminates his labour relations as of the 12th of April, 1994 because he has not been to work. You know that if you stay away from work for five days or more without permission or without valid reasons given, then you are fired from your job. Is that something that is contested?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened or what decision was taken at the Defence Ministry or by Petar Ilic. After February, I didn't go to my workplace any more, and I told you that before. And you yourself can show that I didn't go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says here in the administration document that Aliu Shukri used the first part of his holiday for 1999 on the basis of the decision of the 23rd of March, 1999, what I said a moment ago, and that it shall last 13 working days beginning with the 24th up until the 9th of April, 1999. And he has to report to work on the 12th of April, 1999. I assume that was a Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The individual did not report to work on the day specified, and he did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Milosevic. There was an objection. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, the decision -- this document, in fact, describes that as your leave, your holiday, expired, for which you received a decision, you did not report to work for a full month after that, and that on the basis of the law and the rules and regulations, another decision was made, as it says here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- that your labour relations were terminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One question at a time. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be possible for this document to be shown to the witness so that he could review it and see if he's seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to finish with the cross-examination on these points and then we're going to see if they were to be exhibited. Have you got an English translation of that, Mr. Milosevic, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not have an English translation, but I can hand this decision over to you and leave it with you as evidence and proof that what I asked the witness is correct and that his answer is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll put it on the ELMO then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can have it. Here you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let's put it on the ELMO and have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a two-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, look at that, Mr. Aliu, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- let the witness deal with the document first of all. Have you seen that document before, Mr. Aliu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Since it's been put in front of you, help us, what's the date of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have a look. I can't make out the date very well, but I have never seen this document, ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any comment you would wish to make about it since it's been put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May 1999. No. I have no comment on this document. I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I've ever seen anything of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, the document, as I understand it and as I understand Mr. Milosevic to be alleging, that document is saying that as a result of your absence from work for a particular period of time, your labour relations were terminated, which I take it to mean that you were dismissed from your job. What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to say. As I said before, after 15th of February, I never went to work. And they could -- they could have dismissed me from my work whenever they pleased. They had no problem about that. But I never turned up to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Hand that, if you would, please, to the Prosecution, and then we'll exhibit it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should just like to ask you one more thing, Mr. Shukri, with respect to what we were discussing and linked to the document. What you said was that it is a material fact that you didn't appear at work for a long period of time. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to work after 15th of February. That's the third time I've said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you spent many years working in the state administration, do you know that if you leave your place of employment without any valid explanation or reason, your employment is terminated?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on -- didn't go to work on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all the more so, then. I assume that you were dismissed pursuant to the law. Now, whether you yourself consider that that is a procedure determined by law or whether you were dismissed because you were an Albanian perhaps. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we can take this much further. He's given his account of what happened. You've produced the document. Now, it seems to me there's no point arguing any further about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to your statement now. You said that in 1987, you were subjected to an investigation with respect to the arming of Kosovo Albanians with firearms and that you were taken before a military court in Nis. That is what it says in paragraph 3 of the beginning of your statement. And you say, "I went before the military court in Nis and was found guilty and sentenced to three months' probation." Now, as you were sentenced, although a very lenient sentence because it was a conditional detention period, do you remember what you were found guilty of and sentenced to for three months' probation? For what? What act did you commit? What did it say in the sentence passed by the military court in Nis which you received when you were proclaimed guilty? What was the verdict?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must ask the military court in Nis about that, whether I was guilty or not. If I had been very guilty, I would no doubt have been sentenced to many years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. As you received the sentence and verdict, what did it say in the sentence and judgement, that you were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. found guilty for arming Kosovo Albanians, or did it say something else in the document of the sentence of judgement you received?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was almost two years in front of the military court. This was in 1987. And you can say what you want and write what you want, but I, nevertheless, say that I never saw any of the things that you say happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what things do I say happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Now we're going round and round pointlessly. He has described in his evidence in chief what happened as far as he knows. Now, if you've got something to contradict it with, let's hear it. Otherwise, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my question was: What were you found guilty of? Why were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has told us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- sentenced? What was the verdict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has told us. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, who was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Kosovo, the headquarters where you worked at that time, the TO staff?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ali Muhaxhiri, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, General Ali Muhaxhiri, an Albanian. Precisely. And he didn't receive you after that verdict. He didn't take you back to work at the TO staff, did he?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went to the Provincial Defence Secretariat, where Ismet Krasniqi was my boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say in your statement that you were not allowed to return to the territorial headquarters, as far as I was able to understand. Said, "When my profession was finished I was not allowed to return to the territorial headquarters and to take up -- I was not permitted to carry out the duties I previously performed." That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He said he went on to another job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, you claim that you just read the newspapers in your office. You spent your time reading the newspapers; right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time I read the newspapers. I had no duties at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, then. How did you become informed about the questions and issues that you're testifying about here; from the newspapers or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at my workplace in my office at the secretariat, and the information flowed all the time through the secretariat and to the army corpus [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I didn't understand the end of your sentence from the interpretation, but let's move on. You go on to speak about the Albanian demonstrations in 1981, and you say that the Yugoslav leadership in 1981 considered these demonstrations to be contrary to the state, anti-state demonstrations or words to that effect, something along those lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood you to be explaining that the Yugoslav government or, rather, the Yugoslav leadership took these demonstrations to be anti-state demonstrations in 1981; is that right? Demonstrations against the state; right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the Yugoslav Presidency treated these demonstrations because I wasn't a member of it. I only know that special units of the Interior Ministry came to Kosova in 1981 and operated in Kosova all the time from 1981 until the end of the war. The place where the special units were is called Germija. In 1982, the same unit went to kill Tahir Meha in Prekaz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're talking about the 1980s. Let's make that clear. Not the 1990s. You're not talking about the 1990s, the 1980s; right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered you very well. After 1981, the special units of the Yugoslav Interior Ministry stayed in Germija near Prishtina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, do not become annoyed. It will not help us. Now, Mr. Milosevic, let's have some relevant questions. Do you want to ask the witness about his statement? In which case, he can have a copy in front of him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course he can have a copy in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these questions arise from his statement, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And furthermore, since you don't know what the government of Yugoslavia considered and you say in your statement, in paragraph 5 -- nevertheless, you say the Yugoslav government took these demonstrations to be subversive or something like that, and then you go on to say the Yugoslav police arrived in Kosovo. That is written in line 3 of that same paragraph. "It was at this time that the Yugoslav police came to Kosovo." And then in the next sentence, you say: "After the Serb police entered Kosovo, a lot of Albanian men were imprisoned and the maltreatment, that is mistreatment, of Albanians really became ubiquitous." Tell me, did the Yugoslav police come to Kosovo or was it the Serbian police? In one sentence you say the Yugoslav police came to Kosovo and then, almost in the same breath, you say the Serbian police. Was it the Yugoslav or the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who translated it, but it was the police of Yugoslavia, and all the republics and provinces contributed to that police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means they came from Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Macedonia. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you my answer, and you should know what the Yugoslav police means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say also there were also a lot of murders committed, Albanians -- against Albanian soldiers at the military barracks. What were those murders of Albanian men in military barracks? Please remind me, because although I was in office at the time, I don't remember any murders except for the murder committed by an Albanian man who killed a number of soldiers in military barracks in Paracin. That's the one I remember.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain the matter of the murder of Albanian soldiers in barracks of this degenerate Yugoslav army. There were a number of between 65 and 70 Albanian soldiers killed in the barracks of the Yugoslav army. The case of Aziz Kelmendi was framed. The murder of Aziz Kelmendi in the barracks at Paracin was a scenario prepared by the Yugoslav army. It is impossible for a soldier like Aziz Kelmendi who was on guard in a corridor to reach the arsenal and to -- which was under the command of various officers. A guard in a corridor never had weapons or munitions. You know this very well. You merely wish to stage various --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Now, Mr. Aliu, we must keep this evidence within bounds. Mr. Milosevic, we are not concerned with events in the 1980s, as you know quite well. Now, let's move on to a more relevant period. Have we got the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm going to see if the statements are coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We have copies in English, Your Honour. The statement in B/C/S is on its way as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I wouldn't be asking these questions at all if certain statements were not contained in the witness's own witness statement. Since they are untrue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me explain something. Let me explain something. The fact that something appears in a statement, unless the statement is exhibited, does not mean that it's evidence in the case. Now, you have the right to cross-examine about the statement, and you can do so, and you can have it exhibited if you want. But it does not seem to me to help us very much to have these events of so long ago gone into in enormous detail. What, if I may say, you should concentrate on is the evidence which the witness actually gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We have the statement now in Albania and in Serbian, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the Albanian be put before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have your statement in the Albanian language, Mr. Shukri?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise. There are two statements, both of them in the Serbian language, but the witness reads Serbian, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a photograph of a soldier killed in 1990, Hajrizi from Kuklibeg. I was present at his funeral. One of the cases which you are denying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Aliu, have you got the statement? Now, have the statement in front of you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, what do you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just asked him what were those murders committed against Albanian men in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has dealt with that, and I've told you to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Then you go on to say in the bottom paragraph of this page 2, which is actually the first page of the statement but it is marked 2, quote: "I found out that Milosevic had formed a committee in Kosovo in the spring of 1998 which was named the combat headquarters or combat staff of Kosovo." And then you explain this. What was it; a committee or combat headquarters or staff? Could you explain this in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say spring, and I don't know who translated it into Serbian, but I said in the summer of 1998, there was a joint command formed from which the war staff of Kosova stemmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you formed this personally. And you commanded it and, through it, you received all the information about what was happening in Kosova. You are -- why are you denying it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not here to answer your questions, Mr. Shukri. I am asking you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, you enumerate the members of those combat headquarters or the combat staff. As far as I can see, there were 12 of them. First you say politician Milomir Minic, who was the president of the Socio-Political Chamber. Let's not deal with this mistake now although it is a mistake. It was the Chamber of Citizens in the Yugoslav Assembly. Then you mention Nikola Sainovic, Minic's deputy. You say he had been the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia and Serbia. He was actually Deputy Prime Minister of Yugoslavia. Then you name Zoran Andjelkovic was a member of the headquarters and performed the duties of the president of the government of Kosovo. You actually mean the Executive Council, don't you? Veljko Odalovic was also a member of the headquarters and performed the duties of the Chief of Staff of the district staff of Kosovo. Do you know that he was head of the district in the hierarchy of Serbia's administration? Then you say Vojo Zivkovic was a member of the headquarters, and president of Milosevic's party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you asking a question about Veljko Odalovic? You seem to be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quoting his own statement in order to pave the way for asking him this:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We are talking here about a member of the parliament, member of the federal government, president of Kosovo's government, president of Kosovo's Executive Council, head of the district, chairman of the party organisation in Kosovo. Then General Pavkovic, member of the staff and commander of the so-called army corps of all Serb VJ forces. You enumerate, therefore, people who were all in high public places, high-ranking people and prominent public figures. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why they were part of the staff, and were members of the military staff commanded by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I've already heard about this idea. What I'm interested in is the following: How come you are talking about the clandestine activities of public figures such as the president of the federal parliament, vice-president of the government or head of district in Kosovo? Is it their duty to meet from time to time to discuss issues of importance for the society in general, for the citizens, for the economy? Are they occupying such public offices which require them to meet and discuss these things?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This staff met every Tuesday at 5.00 in the parliament building of Kosova and sometimes in the -- I say this with total responsibility: This staff was appointed by you and was given orders by you for military operations in Kosova, and it used to meet in the army building, and it used to meet in the provincial committee building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me then, Mr. Shukri, what you've just said is also written in your statement at the top of page 3. "The group held regular meetings after it was established, and those meetings were held every Tuesday at 700 hours [as interpreted] on the premises of the Executive Council." That's what you say. Tell me, please, what kind of military or war headquarters is it which meets once a week on Tuesday afternoon at tea time? What kind of war staff is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what -- it's not for him to comment. That is his evidence. That is when they met. Now, whether you say it isn't much of a war staff is a matter for you, but he can't improve on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But is it logical for politicians, high representatives, or should I say the highest representatives, because we're talking about the speaker of the parliament, president of the Executive Council, Prime Ministers, is it logical for them to meet regularly and discuss current issues? Are they forbidden from doing that in the course of performing their public duties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know if you can comment on that. Of course they're not forbidden. I suppose the question can be put in this way: What was there that was unusual, Mr. Aliu, about this particular group meeting? Was it just a normal meeting between politicians and generals or was there something else to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not here a simple question. It's a matter of questions about the military situation in Kosova, and the accused knows this very well. And this staff dealt solely with militaries using Kosova, and in 1998 onwards, this is what they discussed. They weren't there to drink tea in the afternoon, they were here to discuss military issues solely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Every Tuesday at 5.00 p.m.; right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every Tuesday at 5.00 in the afternoon. That was when they met. And if necessary, they also came to the command of the army corps in Prishtina, and were able to sleep in the hotel belonging to the army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Many times in your statement, you accuse Milomir Minic, who was the speaker of the federal parliament, who were allegedly issuing some kind of orders. Do you know that he wasn't even speaker of the parliament as a matter of occupation? It wasn't his profession. He was director, manager of the railways, and he was chairman of the Chamber of Citizens in the parliament. Do you know that that was his real position?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of post you gave him is your problem, but he was member and president of the war staff of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely my point. How can such a number of civilians form a war staff? Even if they were coordinating some activities, how can they possibly make up a war staff? As a military officer with a military education, how can you put so many civilians on a war staff? Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Civil Defence in Yugoslavia had a lot of civilians in it, not just military people per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you think that soldiers belong in a Civilian Protection Unit?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers don't normally belong in such a unit, but they are commanded, and they're commanded by you who were head of -- who was head of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not quite getting your drift now. I was head of the overall defence and Supreme Commander of the army as President of the Republic. Everybody in Yugoslavia knows that. So I don't really understand what you're saying. Would you please care to explain?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I use an example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we put that on the projector?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have this on your monitor or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What is it, Mr. Aliu, you want to explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This the accused can see for himself, the command structure and who was commanding in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be so kind as to give me that paper. I can't see it on the monitor. I don't see very well. I'll put it back on the projector when I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the accused have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What we see here is this: Right there on the top is the Presidency of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, FRY, Supreme Commander of the armed forces. Below that, we see the Ministry of Defence, Federal Secretariat for National Defence, in war called Supreme Command. And then it is divided into the war staff and PVO and command of the army district and the army and naval district. So first we have the Supreme Command, the Ministry of Defence, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then army, navy, and land forces; then land forces is further divided into divisions, corps, and so on and so forth. What are you trying to prove with this? You are saying that there is a Supreme Command, that there are armies, navy, air force, brigades. Will you please translate this and look at it yourself to be able to explain what you are trying to say. You are saying the same thing that is written all over the newspapers, and you are trying to present it to us as something new and spectacular.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour. This document which is my example and which the accused is saying is from a newspaper is from the defence college in Belgrade, and this shows the army military structure in Kosova. This is the main example in which the accused himself can find which unit was under which command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where did you get the document from, Mr. Aliu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is from the faculty, and this is a very important -- this is a very adequate kind of document from the faculty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And was it given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's my document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You say it comes from the faculty. How did it come to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I studied there. I studied at the faculty. This is from the subject about the command and structure of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you got the document when you were studying at the faculty; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, when I was studying at the faculty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When was that, could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1977 to 1981. And this document is, even today, down in the rule book of the Yugoslav armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the -- just a moment. If the Prosecution apply to exhibit it, we will have that document exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please do exhibit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What's the big deal in saying that the army has its own structure, armed forces, that there is a Supreme Command, that there exists the navy, air force, and land forces, and that the land forces further subdivide by army districts, divisions, brigades? What is so important in that so that you should put it to us here? Who has ever denied the existence of air force, navy, land forces, brigades, corps, and who is disputing that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all a comment. He's produced it now, and he says that sets out what he was given in the faculty. Now, you can comment on it if you want, but not now. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's take one of those documents that you gave us yesterday. For instance, a letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have that document and it can be exhibited. If the usher would collect it. We will also have an exhibit number, while we're at it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was exhibited yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, just a moment. We will deal with these two documents now before we go on to other ones. Give that a Defence number, and the other one. It doesn't matter which it is. Whichever is convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The letter regarding Mr. Aliu will be Defence Exhibit 22, and the chart will be Defence Exhibit 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you regarding this letter. It's a letter which the head of administration for defence, Petar Ilic - you showed us this yesterday - sent to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, sector for civilian protection. So in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in its government, there is the Federal Ministry of Defence, and then the area organ in the Republic of Serbia belonging to the defence administration with its Pristina office. That's what's written in the heading. And then the head of defence administration writes to the -- to his superior in the ministry. So he communicates along those vertical lines that you describe and -- is this letter written by him and addressed to the sector in the ministry for civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just read who was it sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says Federal Ministry of Defence, area organ for civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, who was it written to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, which document are you referring to? We've got two. One is numbered 245, the other is 246. They are both dated 28th of July. We could perhaps -- we could perhaps distinguish them by one being longer than the other.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. This is a one-page document, and I'm talking here about the following, that is to say, I want the witness to explain to me whether they are communicating here, that is to say from the head of department to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm not going to go on until I understand which document you're talking about. Now, three documents were put in. Perhaps we can identify them in this way since you're not following the numbers -- no, don't interrupt -- you're not following the numbers. One is described as "Subject: Instructions for the Defence of Inhabited Areas." The next one -- and it's to the defence departments and sections. The next one is to the chiefs of defence departments and head of defence sections. And the third one is described as "Guidelines for the Defence of Inhabited Areas." Now, which of those three is it that you're putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I have in my hands, a paper that is K0004689. That is the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you hand it in and we'll get it compared with the Registry, and we'll see which document it is. We should, in any event, have a record on the transcript of which exhibit you're talking about. Perhaps the registrar could compare the two and say what the number is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused is referring to Exhibit number 248, and it's the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Put that on the ELMO so that the witness can have it too. He can have the original. The accused should have his copy. Yes. Now, what is the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As Mr. Shukri is explaining the organisation, we can see here that the head of the administration, which is an organisational part of the Federal Defence Ministry, is writing to the minister or, rather, to the Ministry of Defence, the sector for civilian defence. Now, I wish to ask you the following: This is the vertical chain of the Federal Defence Ministry; right? Because it goes from the top downwards, from the federal level right down to the local level; right? And we can see here that from the local level --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. Now, can you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The example that we had slightly earlier here but doesn't say who -- that Petar Ilic is addressing personally, Geza Farkas, and he is asking for the arming of the Civil Defence Units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I wish to clarify one point, and that is the functioning of that organisation that you have been talking about. You showed us a schematic of the army a moment ago. Isn't that right, Mr. Shukri? You showed us that diagram; right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You saw very well. Just read carefully who it's addressed to, because you can see the name of that general. Why are you denying it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not denying it, Mr. Shukri. I'm not denying that Geza Farkas at that point in time was the deputy or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not to turn into an argument. Now, ask the question again and let the witness answer it. Just answer the question. Don't get into an argument, Mr. Shukri.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. It is immaterial whether the assistant or Deputy Defence Minister for civilian defence is called in one way or another. The important point and what I wish to establish is that the district organ from Pristina communicates with the assistant Minister of Defence in charge of civilian defence. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we can see who it's written to. Now, what is the point, Mr. Milosevic, of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is the following: I wish to establish whether this is the vertical chain, the line and chain of the Defence Ministry, from top to bottom, that you are talking about. Is it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before that these are the -- this is the vertical chain of command. And you can't deny this. This is merely -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Don't argue with the accused, please. Just answer the questions and we'll get on more quickly. Mr. Milosevic, you've got another ten minutes with this witness. Now, we can see these documents, and we can see --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I haven't even started my cross-examination, Mr. May. Can't you see that the witness has not been answering and cannot in fact answer any question in a proper and correct manner? The witness seems to be quite nervous. Perhaps he ought to calm down first and then proceed to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Don't you make comments either. You've got another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, don't I even have the same amount of time that the opposite side had?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have now had the hour which they had and a bit longer already. Now, you can have -- you can have another quarter of an hour and that will be to -- give you a third more than the Prosecution have had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, are you counting the time that they had on Friday before the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's all been counted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, it's very difficult for me now to get through all the questions I wish to get through in the time that I have because he explained -- went into many explanations here, the kind of explanations that you can read in any newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me this, Mr. Shukri, explain to me this: If this is the vertical chain which the organ of administration goes and in which you yourself worked, what was the vertical chain, for example, for communication in the army? Does it follow the diagram and schematic you showed us a moment ago or does that chain follow a different pattern?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leadership and command is merely a pattern of the kind that I presented before. This is the general scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Petar Ilic was the head of the defence administration belonging to the Defence Ministry, under the Defence Ministry. Who was in command of the army in Kosovo? Who was the main person in the army in Kosovo at that time in 1998, during the time period that you're talking about? Petar Ilic communicated with the Ministry of Defence. Who did the commander of the army communicate with, the corps commander, for example? Let's take the corps commander, who did he communicate with? Let's hear this. You're an officer, so tell me, who does the corps commander cooperate with -- communicate with?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know the answers to these questions very well. You saw in the plan. The commander of the Prishtina Corps answers to the commander of the Nis army. It's very simple. And you are the -- were the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he is responsible to the commander of the army; right? Of course. I'm not asking you because I don't know myself. I wish to establish what you are saying. And to whom is the commander of the Nis army district responsible to? The 3rd Army, who is he responsible to?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is responsible to the chief of the staff of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that we have established two chains of command, one via the organs of the Ministry of Defence from bottom to top which we can see from this letter; the second, you have been explaining, goes from the corps command to the army command, the 3rd Army commander, then the General Staff. That's the military chain of command. Now tell me about the police. Who does the chief of police refer back to? For example, the head of the Internal Affairs Secretariat in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the police matters, you must ask the police. I didn't show you the scheme for the police. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you -- it's not the accused that you're answering to, it's the Court. Now, can you help us with the chain of command of the police or not? If you don't know, Mr. Aliu, say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't in the police to know this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But may we dwell for a moment on these two? That means the following: Is it clear to you, Mr. Shukri, then, that if a part of the organisation of the Ministry of Defence has its vertical line right up to the peaks and if the army goes up to the General Staff - we have established that, right? - how then and on the basis of what grounds can you claim that all these forces are being commanded by some sort of joint command for Kosovo? Or is this a method of work which has to do with civilian defence and mutual information?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me answer the accused again. I explained very clearly the matter of the military districts and the command of the army corps and the provincial Defence Secretariat. Each had their own responsibility, as I explained yesterday. You must not manipulate translations into Serbian. You should know very well that in the event of war, the army was commanded by this joint command which you yourself formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means what you said a moment ago that the corps commander, for example, of Pristina, the Pristina Corps command, is not responsible to the commander of the army and the General Staff and myself but that he is responsible to Milomir Minic. Is that what you're saying? So he receives orders in Milomir Minic and not from the army commander or from myself but from Milomir Minic in Pristina. Is that what you're claiming? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you confusing things? You saw very well the plan that I showed you. Do not try to evade your responsibility. You were the Supreme Commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to stop this. This witness must answer to the Court and not get into arguments with the accused. Just simply say yes or no. Don't argue with him. Now, I've told you, Mr. Aliu. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't give me an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ask it again shortly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The office of command commanding the army, the functions of command, does it go down the chain that you describe from the corps to the army to the Supreme Command and to myself, upwards, or does the command of the army evolve via Milomir Minic? Which is it? Which is what you're claiming here.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm making no claims. I'm merely telling the truth. And I've answered this question three times already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you say so, then it's -- there's no point in continuing along those lines. But is it clear to you that all these documents, all the documents that you have presented here are generally known facts in each local community?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment. It's not a question. It's not a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please. Does it say here in that second document, 4737, on the last page where the tasks of civilian protection, Civil Defence are talked about, units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit 245. Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General purpose CZ units, administer first aid, et cetera. We saw how this functions upwards, then we saw how it functions downwards. Civilian defence. It says: "General purpose units administer first aid, rescue people from destroyed buildings, extinguish initial and minor fires, clean up barricades, organise cleaning and washing of streets," et cetera. Specialised units rescue people in structural collapse emergencies, buildings, roads, et cetera, fire-fighting operations, first aid, destruction of unexploded material, cleaning up the terrain, maintaining law and order, et cetera. They take part in constructing shelters, in ensuring that the population has water supplies, et cetera, et cetera. The monitoring of all terrorist activities. And then mention is made of other operations which the Civilian Protection Unit has with regards to terrorist activities. Now, Mr. Shukri, are you aware, do you know, as you worked in the district organ of the Ministry of Defence in Pristina, how much during that year, and I'm talking about 1998, the year you're testifying about, how many people were killed by the KLA, that is to say Serbs and Albanians and soldiers and policemen, and how many terrorist attacks were launched? How much -- how many settlements had been taken control of, for example, from Orahovac right down the line? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm told that it's in fact 246 we're looking at. At the moment, we're not going to stop to go through that. Whether it's 245 or 246, it matters not. Mr. Aliu, what you're being asked is this: Can you assist the Court by dealing with the number of terrorist attacks, it's said by the KLA, in 1998? If you can help us, say so. If you can't, just say that you can't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to help you. The Court should know. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The KLA did not ever undertake terrorist operations in Kosova. I will only mention one murder: Ilir Durmishi and his friend Tale and Maliq were killed in 1990, and it was never explained who killed them. And the Court knows who was in charge in Prishtina. Can I show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've had much evidence. No, rather than go further. How would you categorise the KLA operations in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The operations of the KLA were a form of defence against the Serbian occupier and barbarian, and a defence of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Next question. You've got another four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Regardless of how you categorise it - and that was your question, Mr. May - do you know how many people, Serbs and Albanians alike, soldiers, policemen, et cetera, were killed by the KLA in the course of 1998? Do you know at least that many people were killed during that period of time? Do you know that at least?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many Albanians were killed by members of the Yugoslav army units, by the police, and by the Serbian special forces units. These were stationed in the -- in the Grand Hotel in Prishtina, the Park Hotel, and the Herzegovina Hotel in Kosovo Polje, and on the main road from Klina to Gjakove --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Shukri --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Would you repeat your question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. Do you disclaim that the KLA in 1998 killed a large number of citizens, Serbs and Albanians, policemen, soldiers, and others? Do you deny that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA did not kill Albanians. On the contrary, it defended Albanians. And the situation in 1998 was a state of war. And you had 50.000 soldiers in Kosova, and we had the right to defend ourselves against colonisation and occupation. Your Honour, would you like to look at just an example, just to look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Put it on the ELMO quickly. Yes, Mr. Aliu, what is it? This is a report, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a statement by the general of the Prishtina army corps who says that there are 150.000 armed men in Kosova, whereas the accused talks of terrorist groups which didn't exist at all, or if they did exist, they were Serbian terrorists. And here we have special units being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the Prosecution want to take that further, they can. If you'll give that document back to the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Your last question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, give it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give that back to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, well, it's pointless to cross-examine this witness who, in his statement here, says where the Park Hotel is located and the Grand Hotel, and who claims that Ojdanic was the chief of the General Staff, that Pavkovic was the commander of the 3rd Army, that I was the Supreme Commander, and he could see all that on television and hear it over the radio, read it in the papers, and it's no secret. So how can I examine a witness, especially with the help of the other side there who's sitting there triumphantly, pulling out certain documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Mr. Wladimiroff, have you any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Witness, you studied military sciences at the faculty, the military faculty, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence faculty at Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So I take it that you would know the difference between an official state of war and any armed conflict, would you not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was there an official state of war in Kosovo before the NATO bombing started?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was that declared --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me use this opportunity. On the third day of the Rambouillet agreement, there was a general mobilisation of the Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does that imply an official state of war?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So am I right in thinking that an official state of war wasn't declared by the Yugoslav authorities?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a state of war. But it was secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What do you mean by a "secret"? Was it not declared in public?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not published publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And why do you say a secret? How would you know if it was secret?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because the mobilisation at the Defence Secretariat took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was it in that mobilisation disclosed that there was an official state of war?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So we can read it if you would have that order, would we not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an order of this kind because it was a secret order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But how would you know if you don't have that order?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Have you seen that order?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw how the mobilisation summonses were being prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And have you seen that order?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Again, how would you know that in that order there was secretly announced an official state of war?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because conscripts were called up and also the conscripts in the police units were also mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Last question: In your testimony, you say that in the event of war, then the army would be commanded by the structure that you gave evidence about. Would you agree that if there was no state of war, that the whole structure would not function and did not function, although it was in place?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI ALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- if there were not war, if it were a state of peace, no doubt it would not operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On reflection, no re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before we go on, we need to renumber an exhibit, the organigramme schematic, as it was called. It will be renumbered as a Prosecution Exhibit. If the registrar would give us the figure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, formerly marked Defence Exhibit 23 will now be Prosecutor's Exhibit 249.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we will need to deal -- I don't think you're dealing with Colonel Crosland, but we need to deal with that, if you would tell Mr. Ryneveld, before we finish today. Perhaps at the end of today we will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know that the information upon which the application that I imagine you're referring to is mounted won't actually be arriving in written form until after 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it's the original application under 92 bis. We need to straighten it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In light of his protected status, can he take a seat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Sit down to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has been granted various protective measures. In those circumstances, may he please have this piece of paper. Could you show it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just look at this piece of paper. Don't read out what is on it, but if the details contained on it are accurate, please say, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that piece be paper please be produced and given an exhibit number. Your Honour, the witness will deal with a number of sites of involvement by the unit with which he was engaged, briefly, and to make his evidence more intelligible to not only the Court but also the public, I will identify the areas by reference to the atlas that we have been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. using. If a version of that may be available, I will be able to -- I'll point out the pages from time to time. If the usher could help us when I -- it won't be immediately. When I specify a page, if she can simply place it on the overhead projector. He will then be dealing with one area in much greater detail, for which a special map has been prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You will be known throughout these proceedings as Witness K25. I'm going to deal with matters of background shortly, and where possible, if you can answer questions simply with a yes or no, it will save time and make the administration of your evidence that much more compact. K25, are you a Serbian police officer, having had compulsory military service with the JNA in the course of which you trained as a short-range anti-tank self-guided rocket operator as part of a JNA infantry battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After military service, did you complete studies to the university level, becoming a police reservist and later working for the police, after further training becoming a member of a unit known as the PJP or police special unit, continuing with ordinary police work but performing special assignments for the PJP on certain occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the unit of which you were an occasional member receive instruction from the VJ on specialist weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, for training purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of the specialist weapons on which you were trained by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: During training, we had compulsory training in operating infantry weapons, military equipment, weapons of medium range such, as Zolja and Osa, hand-held rocket launchers, land-mines, basic training in operating special weapons of higher calibre, such as 12.9, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these weapons then available to your unit as and when required?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, because that fell within the framework of training in handling infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I move to paragraph 6. Were you deployed from the place where you were based to Kosovo on several occasions in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. On six occasions in 1998 and once in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will deal briefly with the occasions in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would be good enough, please, to open the map at map 5, 0-5 on the left-hand corner there, laying that on the overhead projector. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This shows west-central Kosovo. And was your first deployment in the Kosovska Mitrovica, Srbica, Josanica and Klina area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In a sentence, please, the nature of the operation of the PJP then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The purpose of the operation was to free or liberate roads from Srbica and Klina and Klina to Pec because Albanian terrorists at the time had sealed off roads in this area and carried out constant terrorist operations in those sections of the road and shot at anything that moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can't see Klina, but it's a little further south on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can't see Klina but it's a little further south on the map. Thank you very much. We can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The date of that deployment, please, Witness K25?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Sometime around the 1st of March, I believe, or the 21st. I can't remember exactly. In fact, it was -- it was definitely the 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, had there been any earlier deployments of this kind or was this the first of its kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: There had been no previous deployments. Our unit had never gone out into the field to perform such tasks. This was our first anti-terrorist assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second deployment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second deployment, same area, was when and to do what, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The second time, we went to the same positions, and our task was to ensure that the road was passable. Our presence had the purpose of securing that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The date of this second deployment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: After the completion of the previous task, we had three or four days' leave and then we came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We now go to map page 4, please, the previous page. And the lower part of it, I think. We will see Pec and Decani. Your third deployment, Witness K25, was when, where, and to do what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Our third deployment followed immediately after the second one, after a short break. It was on the road from Pec to Djakovica, where again Albanian terrorists had cut off sections of that road, preventing normal traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see on the map, if we look south of Pec and north of Decani - I don't know if it's possible to focus in on the bottom right-hand corner - we can see a couple of villages called Donji Streoci and Gornji Streoci, I think. Did they feature in this, your third deployment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. That means that if we were not on our regular two days' leave, we were at our positions in Gornji Streoci where we were securing communications, that is, roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we move to the fifth -- I beg your pardon, the fourth deployment, where was the fourth deployment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: On our fourth assignment, we tried to establish control over Jablanica, which was a stronghold of the terrorists where around 3.000 well-armed terrorists were based. However, at that time we failed to enter the area of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is Jablanica in the south of Kosovo, considerable distance away from the previous deployments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Map 15, and the top left-hand corner of it, shows Jablanica, and it is right at the southern end or edge of Kosovo. No. Map 15. I don't think we're looking at the right map there. No. That's not the right map. Page 15. Oh, dear. Top left-hand corner. Let's have a look at it. No. The top left-hand corner. Keep going. The witness will point it out for you. We can see the borders there of Kosovo and we can see Jablanica right at the top left of the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long did this unsuccessful mission last, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Every field deployment lasted between 25 and 30 days, but this attempt to take Jablanica lasted for about a day or a day and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could move to the fifth deployment. I think we're going to want to turn to map --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we turn to the fifth deployment, I think we're going to be turning to map 9, which is on central -- the far west of Kosovo. And was your fifth deployment, and it's the top of the map, just south of Decan? Thank you. Perfect. And did your fifth deployment take you to the area of Prilep and Junik, and in particular, to the village of Baboloc, which we can just see towards the right and towards the lower part of the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did this deployment involve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Just holding the road, securing the road, the communication line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally, the sixth deployment, also on map 9, was, I think, on the road between -- no. It was in the area of Junik, which we can see just almost in the centre of the screen, towards the bottom. And what was that sixth deployment all about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: We were supposed to take control over that village from which there had been constant terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would be good enough now just to take -- open the map up and to put the left hand -- the right hand part of one page in the -- that's the stuff. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of this operation, did you have some assistance from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion we received support from Lake Radonjic on the part of the army of Yugoslavia VJ, because the Albanian terrorists in that area had a very strong base, were very strongly fortified.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that lake is shown as the blue part of the right-hand map shown on the overhead projector, I think. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can now move from paragraph 8, for convenience. We'll come back to paragraph 9, but move over to paragraph 15 in order that things can be dealt with sequentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we come to your operation in 1999, the previous ones, giving the pattern of your unit's involvement, albeit in 1998. Did you, in 1999, find yourself deployed to the Velika Krusa/Mala Krusa area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for this and for the witness's observations in relation to this deployment, we have a special map that's been produced in two different sizes, one for placing on the overhead projector and the slightly larger size version for Your Honours, the accused and the amici. May that now be produced and distributed, please. And, Your Honours, if you want, of course, to find these areas on the atlas or to make a cross reference, then Velika Krusa is on map 10, it's map reference K23, but I think having identified it in that way, we can rely on this more detailed map for the balance of the evidence on this topic. Can the usher put the small version on the overhead projector, and I think the -- if we get it so that it's central to the projector. Thank you very much. Then I think the experts in the booth will be able to focus on what we require.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pseudonym name sheet will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 250, and this map will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 251.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness K25, the markings on this map, which we will interpret in due course, were they put on at, as it were, your direction, reflecting the things that you were observing and able to tell us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When was this deployment? When did it start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, in the early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The booth may wish to move to the junction or towards the junction of the two green lines. Thank you very much. That's enough. And at the left hand join of those two green lines, we see the village or town of Zrze.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was your PJP unit deployed to the area of Zrze on the Djakovica-Prizren road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We arrived there on that day from Baboloc village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to deal with the identification of units, with the Chamber's leave, at the end of the session in a short Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. private session, and I'll remain anonymous as to units for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you arrived there with your unit, what level of equipment did you have, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: We arrived with three 110 trucks, one Pinzgauer, three jeeps, one armoured jeep, three civilian trucks, and our own usual weaponry that is normally in our possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have contact or did your unit have contact with a VJ officer? If so, at what time, on what date, and tell us a little about what that encounter led to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. This gentleman from the army of Yugoslavia met us, and instead of directing us to Zrze, he deployed us along the road. And together with our company commander, he established a link along this line of blockade, that is, deployed us there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for this microphone to be turned on for us, too, not only for the interpreters, because I almost can't hear the witness. I can't hear what he's saying. I have the impression that this microphone is turned on only for the interpreters' booths. I can hardly hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or if you use this headphone, you can easily -- you can hear them quite loud and clear.
