utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Serbian is not interpreted into Serbian, Mr. Kwon. This witness is not being interpreted into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can hear the Serbian channel. And apparently there's no other way of improving it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear the Serbian channel very well when you are speaking but not when the witness is speaking. I can hear him from the headphones, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you try once? You can try once.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you that I can hear it from the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that those microphones should be turned towards the witness, those microphones which are now facing you, not the witness. Then I will be able to hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Those in charge of this will organise it as best they can. There's nothing more that we can do about it. The Registry have heard what you've said, and if there is any improvement that can be made, it will be made. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The particular nature of the distortion - pity the accused hasn't followed this - means that different microphones have to be used and that's why he can only get it through the headphones, which he declines to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness K25, would you be good enough, please, to reflect what you've described about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Reflect what you've described about your deployment with reference to the map and to the coloured lines. Use the pointer and just show where you were deployed, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: From the point where the junction is between the railroad and the road, along the main road from Djakovica to Prizren, in Mala Krusa and in this general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The VJ -- the VJ officer to whom you've referred, what was your understanding as to his -- the breadth of his authority over the equipment of the various units or the units that were deployed in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: He was in command only of the armed vehicles that were together alongside us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What level of communication was there between the units - and you might be able to give us an account of the number of units - the units deployed there, and what level of communication between your unit and the VJ units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Communication between the police forces was conducted through radio communication on the same channel, and with the VJ, we had oral control because they didn't have radio communication stations with the same channels as us. Should the need arise, we would be able to contact the staff, our headquarters, who did have a radio communication with the army if we needed to contact the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The operation on which you were engaged, again looking at the map, using the pointer, and expressing it in straightforward terms, was to achieve what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The object of the operation or, rather, the operation itself took place in various stages. This was the first preparatory stage where the basic goal was from the Bela Crkva access, repel the terrorists towards Malisevo and Milanovici and to pull out the civilian population from the line of fire. Everything was done with a greater goal in mind, and that was that the terrorists had large control over the territory which was very inaccessible. And we feared a NATO descent. And so in order to reduce this and to ensure that we had control over the area, this is the kind of operation we engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Malisevo is not actually shown on this map. It can be found on map 10, although don't turn to it, and it is simply to the north and east slightly of the area shown on this map. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In general, and later we'll come to particulars, but in general, what happened to civilians within this area of operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I'm not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll try again. In general, what happened to the civilians in this area of operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: With the start of the operation, the civilians were in the area, and as there was action between us and the KLA, the civilians would -- pulled out of the area of operations towards the communication line and road between Djakovica and Pec. So they were displaced from Mala Krusa, the ultimate point of the operation, for their own safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in what direction were they sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: In the direction of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: But outside Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you ever discover what happened to them after that or was that for others to speak of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now can we deal with the movement of civilians in a little more detail? To whom -- I beg your pardon. Did you involve yourself directly in identifying and moving civilians, and if so, to whom or to what unit did you hand civilians over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: As we held the line and the blockades, all the civilian population left from the in-depth positions from the Celine village, where they were directed by our own forces outside the zone of operations towards Mala Krusa and the railway station, and all the civilians were handed over to the local policemen, the local police force, who due to their previous experience in which the KLA would dress in civilian clothing, disguising themselves and hide with the civilian population, we would hand them over to the local MUP, and they would know who the members of the KLA amongst them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Roughly how many civilians did you hand over to the local MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I can't give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate? You have done in the statement, but can you give us an estimate now that you're here in court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: About 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When handed over, were women and children treated in any way differently from the way in which the men were treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Although it was a very hot day, the women and children were put up in the -- at the railway station in Mala Krusa, and then the Prizren SUP organised transport for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the men, was transport organised for them or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right that you and some of your colleagues made provision for some of those people to have water, where otherwise they would not have had water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I don't understand why they wouldn't have had water otherwise. We policemen were there. They were our citizens, and they got water. And we organised ourselves in such a way as to place a policeman up on the road, by the road, and as the military forces crossed this road very quickly because of the operations going on, we positioned a policeman to look after the children while they were running across the road to a building where there was drinking water to be had. And we gave them about 5.000 litres of water, to all of them. We distributed this water amongst them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The local MUP, were they deployed in one particular place or were they interspersed along the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: They had their own point up at the junction in Mala Krusa, towards Beli Drim and along the elevation to the right of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that their only place of deployment, on that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Well, they also had their positions in the village of Zrze and in the village by the bridge. Its name is -- let me just think. Rogovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they have checkpoints at these places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. I forgot to say that they had their checkpoint also in Velika and Mala Krusa. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 19. What was the role, if any, of local Serb reservists in particular villages in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: They protected themselves, defended themselves, because there weren't enough police to go around to protect each and every Serb village or, rather, all Serbs in Albanian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were they armed, and did they have uniforms to reflect their reserve police status?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They were all in the reserve police force. They were all reserve policemen, and they all had both uniforms and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn to cooperation at this exercise or operation between VJ and the MUP. The VJ officer whom you've already spoken of, of what was he in charge, as it appeared to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: For his combat vehicles only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there an involvement by members of your PJP group with his units on a so-many-people-per-armoured-vehicle basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. We would supply the physical protection of those armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the protection being provided appear to be part of a pre-existing arrangement or plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No. It was part of an agreement in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 21. At what time did the operation begin and on what date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The 25th of March, between 5.00 and 5.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the deployment was along the road you've spoken of. Was it also along the road from Zrze to Bela Crkva and the wine factory near Orahovac which we can see as the top of the two green lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Well, that should be it, but I wasn't there so I didn't see it, but our people were supposed to have been there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps now is the time to look at the key on the map, which is at the bottom part of the map, if the usher would be good enough so that we could see what's what. First let's look at the key, if you can focus on that. A little bit further. A teeny bit further. You can always fold the map in half if it's going to obstruct the lens. If we can just look at the key, please. The green -- the continuous green line is said, on this map which you have -- in the annotation of which you have participated, is said to be the 23 Vojvodina PJP Detachment. The continuous dark blue line is the Prizren MUP. The dotted blue line is the Nis PJP Detachment. The double blue line, now off the map, but don't worry, we'll come to it later, is said to be Frenki's JSO. And then there's another mark simply saying "VJ," and then there's an arrow giving the deportation route, which we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the deployment of -- no, I'll ask the question the other way round. Which of these units did you see yourself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could start with which unit was his.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which unit was yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: My unit, that is to say, we were within the frameworks of the 23rd Detachment, it was the 7th Company, along the communication from Zrze to Mala Krusa, on the Djakovica to Prizren road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so that deployment was something you knew of personally yourself. Did any of these other deployments that you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I have one correction to make, if I may. The special units or JSO, units for special operations, I did not include in the sense of them taking part in the operations but merely that I saw them during the following operations. And the route taken by the refugees was not one that I drew in, but that was the general direction that they moved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll come to the JSO in a couple of minutes. Going back to where we were on the south part of the markings of the map, the green line, then, running along the road is your own unit. As to the Prizren MUP, to the left or the north-west of that, is that something you saw yourself or simply learnt of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then further north of that, the deployment reflected by the next green line marked as the 23rd Vojvodina PJP Detachment and running up to Orahovac, did you see that yourself or simply learn of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I know they were there. It was a component part of the cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Nis Detachment, shown by the blue broken line, was that something you saw yourself or something that you learnt of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Once again, part of the cooperation. I knew they were there, but I didn't actually see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally, as you've already told us, further north on the map - if the usher would be so good - the double blue line respecting -- reflecting Frenki's JSO, a unit you saw, but later, I think you've told us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I just met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, that's the deployment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the deployment of the various units. Your instruction came from whom and at what level as to what you were to do? Don't specify the person, but give us the rank of the person from whom your instructions came.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: At the level of the company, instructions were received from the main officer in command, and the information was sent down to the commanders of the companies and the companies would relay them to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First sentence of paragraph 25, for the Court. The objective of the operation was to do what to the terrorists, the underlying purpose, as explained to you, being what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: To free the communication between Djakovica and Prizren, which is where there were constant attacks by the KLA, and to push back the members of the KLA towards Malisevo, to pull out the civilian population from the zone of operations, which is something that was done in each and every operation. The civilian population would be pulled out from the combat zone. Two groups would see to this. That is to say, the operations were between us and the KLA. And the larger plan was to diminish the territory under KLA control because of the possibility of NATO troop landings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: According to instructions given, what was the estimate of the number of KLA in the area? What did you think of the number given? Did you have your own estimate, however rough, of how many there may have been there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Well, a basic assessment was 10.000 terrorists. And we considered amongst ourselves that there were far less, perhaps five.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've dealt with the deployment in general terms. Can you just help us in detail with the deployment of tanks in the area and also the vehicles called BOVs, BOVs. First of all, tanks. Where were there tanks in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: One tank was up at the bridge. Another tank was here in this settlement, Velika Krusa, and three tanks were to our right at our ultimate positions in Mala Krusa. And four BOV armoured vehicles were deployed between Mala and Velika Krusa along the road, running between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it may be obvious, but to which units did tanks and BOVs belong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: They belonged to the army of Yugoslavia. The police did not have this kind of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 26. Did you personally see anything of the way in which villagers were moved from their villages or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: As to the movement of villagers or their removal, I didn't see that, and I didn't hear that they went out, that they left Velika and Mala Krusa at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 28. You've told us already about the system in general for movement of men, women, and children, and the movement via Mala Krusa railway station, I think, but help us with this: Between the 24th and 27th of March, what sort of numbers of people did you see passing through Mala Krusa railway station, and were they just from Mala Krusa or did they come from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, I was not there, so I don't know about that particular date, but when I was there, which is from the 25th onwards, about 5.000 refugees went by, not more, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second part of my question was were they all from Mala Krusa or did they come from other places? And if so, by what routing had they reached this particular railway station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I didn't talk to them as to where they were coming from, but nobody came from Velika or Mala Krusa, they came from the village road from the direction of the village of Celine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 29. Again, you've told us in general terms of how people moved, vehicles for the women and children or on foot for the men, but were there any examples of the men being moved in trucks from the railway station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases like that. But these were cases when several vehicles were sent on or the vehicles were free, and people were taken that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which body was responsible, as you could judge it, for the transportation, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The SUP, Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you learn or understand that it was the SUP, the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, that was responsible for this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. transportation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Nobody expected such large numbers of refugees at that point in time, so we informed the SUP of Prizren of what we were facing, and through radio communication they told us to put them up at the railway station from whence transportation would be organised for them outside the combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The transports that were provided, were they driven by uniformed or un-uniformed men or women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Mostly uniformed persons, whereas others wore just parts of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the KLA who were being driven out, was there a route available for them to move along? Was it usual or unusual for such a route to be available for the KLA dealt with in operations of this sort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. Every time there were alternative directions, because usually there were small-scale operations under way within the frameworks of a larger operation, and they were all pushed back to a given territory. And that is why alternative directions were left open and these people were steered towards a desired position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The PJP company headquarters in the village of Mala Krusa, give us an example, please, of the degree of -- degree to which that headquarters was armed. What equipment did it have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: They had small arms, their own personal weapons, plus an armoured vehicle with an M-84 machine-gun, 12.7 millimetres -- 7.9 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they have any armoured vehicles available to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please now deal with a couple of particular incidents. On the morning of the 25th, at about 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning, did you witness the capture of some Albanian men in the area of the -- on the Djakovica-Prizren road or in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom were they captured? What happened to them initially?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: They were captured by our company along that road. I don't know exactly how because I didn't see it myself. I don't know where exactly they were caught but they were brought into us. They had visible KLA insignia, and between them they had one rifle made in China. And I handed them over to the local police, which was based 30 metres away from us, because those were the orders we had. So they never entered our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to them after they'd been handed over by you to the local MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. Three local policemen took them along the road towards Beli Drim, into some houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think - and the witness will confirm this if I'm correct - Beli Drim may not be indexed in your atlases, but it is in fact the blue river, I think, that runs just to the south and west of the green markings on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would that be correct, Witness K25?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So taken towards that river, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No, not towards the river. In the direction of the river. From the road, along the road towards the river, and then they took a left turn about 30 metres away towards -- to a field of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened after that to the men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: After that, we heard rifle fire, and we all thought, at the same time, that one of them had tried to escape. But we didn't pay attention that much. Two local policemen returned to the road, and one of them was still gone. At the same moment, our colleagues brought another three members. I don't know -- I'm not sure about two of them, but one of them I know had KLA insignia. And they handed them over to those two local MUP members. Just then, the third local policeman turned up, and together they took them away to a house which was about six metres away from that checkpoint, and when these policemen again returned several minutes later, we realised that nobody was guarding the captives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see the captives, either the six or the three, ever again alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see any of them dead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I can't say precisely whether it was them, but I went to that house where they had been taken, and I saw bodies of men. I didn't count them, and I cannot positively identify them, I can only assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that to the house where the three had been taken or are you referring to the place where the six had been taken? And how long after the events you've recently described was it that you went and saw the dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely whether it was on the same day or the following day. I don't know. But it was the place where the six had been taken. I never entered the place where the three had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the bodies distributed in an orderly way on the floor or were they piled up or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Some were piled one on top of another. One was laying away from the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following your observations of the six men and the three but before you went to the place where the six men had been taken, did you have some concerns for a local family of Kosovo Albanian villagers in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Explain why you became concerned and what you did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Well, after this incident, a doubt arose in my mind that those people might have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to the particular local villagers, tell us about where they were and why you had concerns for them or what you were troubled might happen to them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: They were about five metres away from our headquarters. And when we were shielding our vehicles under their awning, they helped us. And we were shielding our vehicles because NATO was targeting military vehicles and other targets. What else do you want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you do so far as this family was concerned, or extended family? I think it was a place in -- it was a compound, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. They lived in a compound behind us. And on one occasion one of the three local policemen I had mentioned before asked us to go inside. In fact, he asked, first of all, whether there was anyone inside. We said no, but he didn't believe us and tried to enter himself. So I went inside with him. He saw all the six houses, and he even talked to some of the male inhabitants in the Albanian language, but from their conversation, I noticed that some threat must have been issued because I saw fear in their eyes and in their overall demeanour. He asked us to hand over all the men to them, and I refused. There ensued a quarrel between the two of us, whereupon he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can give us an idea of the comparative strength of forces. There were three MUP officers but how many men were there deployed together with you at this particular location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: According to our positions, there was supposed to be only the headquarters. However, there was this armoured vehicle which had been attached to us. So we were 11 in total. Everybody had their own specific assignment. So at any given moment, we were six or seven on the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us that anxiety appeared on the face of the residents within that compound following conversation in the Albanian language. Did you speak any Albanian at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later that evening and as night fell, what arrangements did you make with your local commander so far as those local residents, and it may be other local residents, were concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Since we were concerned for their safety, we suggested -- or, rather, we agreed that this entire family who lived within this compound including six houses, move to a house close to us so that we could protect them more easily. We were not able to control the entire compound, and it was quite possible for the local policemen to come and enter the compound from a different direction without us seeing them. They accepted this suggestion and moved into the first house closest to us, and we asked them for women and children to move into one room and the men to occupy another room because we couldn't have complete confidence in them after all. And the men were asked, before going to the bathroom, to report to the guard to say that they were going to use the toilet. And that's the way it worked. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Until the following morning when what happened? Deal with it quite briefly, please. Paragraphs 40 and 41.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following morning, what happened to the people in this house? What suggestions did you make? What, actually, did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: They didn't do anything. I don't quite understand what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the morning, did you speak to the family leaders of the group you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I told them that the situation is what it is and that when we leave, nobody will be left to guarantee their safety. And we had already had a word about the possibility of being transferred away from there, so we suggested that they go to a Catholic village across the Beli Drim river because nobody ever shot from a Catholic village at the police, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and consequently, the police never entered a Catholic village. They accepted this, and they asked if they were allowed to take their belongings with them. Of course we told them they could take whatever they liked. And we just warned them that Beli Drim --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, it's not a river.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: -- is very high, so they should go by tractor. One of them asked if he could take his excavator, and we advised him not to because somebody might think he would be using it to dig a bunker or something of that kind. He accepted this advice and did not drive an excavator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How, in the event, did they leave their compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: At the moment when they were ready to go and we were packing too, local policemen started towards Beli Drim too. And we told them they should better wait until the policemen come back, because we cannot guarantee the safety. When the local policemen returned, they demolished the back wall of the compound and went out into the junction so as not to be seen, and left. And 15 minutes later, we left that place too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There may be some ambiguity in the form of your answer as interpreted. When you say "they demolished the back wall," are you referring to the local policemen or to the local inhabitants who were leaving the compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The inhabitants who were leaving their compound, because the policemen didn't know how to drive excavators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you're moving on to another topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It being a convenient moment, we will adjourn. Witness K25, we're going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Could you remember in this adjournment and any others there may be in your evidence not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that includes members of the Prosecution. Would you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're on paragraph 42. But just before we move on to the few matters of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've used the phrase mop-up, I think, in relation to this operation. Can you just describe what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: It's just a phrase in the Serbian language. A mop-up operation is considered to involve pushing back the KLA from a certain territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Picking up your narrative, was there an incident of confrontation between your commander and local MUP over the robbing of refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. That happened at the intersection in Mala Krusa going towards Beli Drim. On that occasion, three members of the local MUP tried to rob the refugees who were moving in a column. And the company commander, who was held at gunpoint by those three local policemen, was forced to put on his rank insignia. And when we approached and cocked our weapons at them, these three local policemen backed away and eventually did not carry on with their intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 26th of March, were you positioned at the Mala Krusa junction or thereabouts, and what did you see of a flow of refugees on that day? Just tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: They came all the time, in smaller and larger groups. There was a constant, intense flow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've -- perhaps I'll come back to paragraph 45 a little later. Can we just deal with uniforms at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit 18, please. I'm sorry I hadn't asked for it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While that's being produced, what uniforms did the 23rd PJP wear at the time of this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The PJP wore green camouflage uniforms with visible PJP insignia on their right shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is actually part of paragraph 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, was there a practice of wearing ribbons, and if so, tell us a little bit about it. First, was there such a practice, and why were ribbons used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. During this operation, four colours were used in the form of ribbons; yellow, red, blue, and white in various combinations. And the reason was that KLA members were known to sometimes wear our uniforms, invite policemen to approach them, and then kill them. Therefore, we wore ribbons in order to be able to recognise one another. And there were code books, changed on a daily basis, so that everyone knew which colour were to be -- which colours were to be worn that day. And members of other units did not have PJP insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you wear ribbons with your PJP green uniform or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Because there were certain emblems of the PJP for the purpose of identification. Everybody knew that our emblems and insignia could not be easily procured, gotten hold of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this operation, what uniform was the local MUP wearing and what was the local - if there was a local - PJP wearing? And look at the photograph, if you find help in that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The local MUP wore blue camouflage uniforms, and the local PJP did the same, but in addition, they also had their own PJP vests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is it suggested that there was any local PJP members?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us? Was there a local PJP presence here as well as your own from outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Not during this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But generally in other operations, was there a local PJP presence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Every SUP had their own PJP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Witness K25, when you are referring to local MUP, does it mean the reservist or is it different from those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of them were part of the local MUP, both active duty and reserve policemen. And as to what units they belonged to, I don't know. I don't even know whether they were active duty or reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit 18 on the overhead projector, does any of these photographs show uniforms of the local MUP or, when in deployment, the local PJP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: This would be the local PJP, local uniform, and the PJP uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Photograph 6, I think, was the one pointed out. And I think that it can be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought it was 7 he was pointing out. Could you point again, please, Witness K25, the PJP and also the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] PJP is this one. Local police and local PJP is this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, the first was number 7, the second was number 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although it doesn't necessarily mean that the local PJP is depicted in this picture, because there were moments when we, too, wore blue camouflage uniforms. We didn't on this occasion, but on some previous occasions we did wear such uniforms, together with our own vests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I, in order to try to deal with things so far as possible chronologically, keep in reserve our return to paragraphs 45, 7, and 8, and just cast ourselves back a little bit to paragraph 9 just to conclude various operations before dealing with general matters. So paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from the operation you've already told us about, were there other operations in which you were involved, on which your unit was involved, in particular one in Orahovac in late March, early April of 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. We took part, after Mala Krusa, in the next destination, which was in Orahovac towards Milanovici, over the hill. Towards Milanovici across Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did the general scheme of that operation compare with the one you've given us in more detail, Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. How do you mean how did the scheme compare with?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the Orahovac operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The purpose of the operation was to continue the operation in Mala Krusa under the wings of the large-scale cooperation which was aimed at pushing the terrorists back to Milanovici and towards the village of Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we've seen in your marked map for Mala Krusa a box shape of deployments of troops, an open box shape. Do you know one way or another if a similar format was used in the next mission or operation at Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I don't remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One detail about the Orahovac mission or operation: What if any VJ support was provided to your group on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. The support provided was with mortar fire, 120-millimetre mortar fire, because we were under fire ourselves. And the terrain was highly inaccessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard about your -- I'm not going to trouble with paragraph Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 10. Paragraph 11. We've heard about your detachment. Just give us an idea, please, of its size. Of how many companies was the 23rd Detachment composed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: It had ten companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Each of how many men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Between 150 and 180 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I move over from paragraph 12 to paragraph 13. In the operations that you've described for us, how were instructions communicated at the really local -- the sub-unit level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You were, I think, a sub-unit. How did your commander give you instruction so that you knew where to go and to some degree what to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Only orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you given any documentation or maps or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Only cards when operations were under way, so that we knew where our own forces were and that there wouldn't be any crossfire between us, but no other written document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those cards, what other units did they identify for the very purpose of avoiding crossfire, typically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: All the units which took part in the cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would that include the VJ or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So how did you know where the VJ were? How did you know how to avoid problems of crossfire so far as they were concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Because the army of Yugoslavia was deployed along the same positions that we had taken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as you've already explained, you were able to communicate with them orally or via your headquarters as required; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. Or through radio communication. But once again, only orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, then. If we can just conclude by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can conclude by going back to the end of the summary, page 9, paragraphs 45, 46, and 47. You've shown us on the marked map which has now left the screen - perhaps it can go back - but you've shown us how Frenki's JSO were seen by you and I think you said at a later stage north of the immediate area of operation surrounding Mala Krusa. Do you actually know where they were deployed at the time of the Mala Krusa operation itself or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I don't know, no. All I know is that we met them at one point, but I don't know either where they were deployed or whether they took part in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how many days after the operation itself was it, approximately, that you saw them in the area indicated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I didn't see them in the area of Velika and Mala Krusa, if you mean the operation there; I didn't see them there. I saw them by Orahovac behind Vrana Stijena. We just met, and for about ten minutes I saw them for that length of time, but other than that I didn't have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But how many days after the operation did you see them there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: If you consider Velika and Mala Krusa to be the operation, then two days after the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 46. By -- by whom and from where were MUP units in Kosovo commanded so far as you could judge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The command structure of MUP is something that I'm not acquainted with exactly, but we did know quite simply that there was a Crisis Staff of MUP in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to coordination with the VJ, you've touched on this to some degree already, but in operations where the VJ were involved, what can you say or from what can you infer the level of coordination for VJ operations or for operations in which the VJ were involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I can't make any conclusions as to that, but I knew, though, that the army was a territorial area, and it did not coincide with the SUP areas so that military representatives had to be present when an operation was decided upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. When, in your experience, MUP and VJ were involved together, was there a lead organisation? If so, which was the lead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: The army of Yugoslavia just offered its support, whereas we undertook anti-terrorist operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever attend or even just see operational planning sessions? If so, what representation was there, if any, by VJ at such sessions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just private session for the last matters, if we may, on the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You work in the police force as deputy police chief of a large town in our country; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Well, it's not such a large town, it's a medium-sized town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were you by rank during these events that you have testified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I was a sergeant -- corporal, beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you receive your promotions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I got a higher rank from you or, rather, from the minister of the internal affairs at that time, and this was a promotion for exceptional efforts and commendation towards the homeland and the police force. And later on, I was appointed sergeant and then captain. Lieutenant and captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all this happened after I was brought to The Hague, isn't that right? And you mentioned commendation and, as far as I know, the commendation you received was for bravery, for courage, isn't that right, during the war, during the NATO aggression; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You went to Kosovo for the first time in March 1998. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness 25, could you put a pause between the answer and question so that the interpreters could follow. You understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So March 1998, you went to Kosovo for the first time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was an operation under way at the time because the Albanian terrorists had cut off the roads between Srbica and Klina and between Pristina and Klina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this correct too: That the police at that time was waging anti-terrorist operations in Kosovo which were caused by the fact, triggered off by the fact that terrorist attacks had been launched on everything that moved along the roads, on everything and anything moving along roads? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, that's what we did, anti-terrorist work. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the area you were in yourself, there were terrorist bases there in Gornje Prekaze and Donje Prekaze and Ovcarevo; isn't at that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the zone in which the police forces were operating was within that triangle exclusively. That is to say within the triangle where the terrorist bases were located; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you got there, you were told to hold those positions or to protect and defend a certain road, the Klina to Srbica road, in fact, and that the Albanian terrorists would probably shoot at you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was what your first assignment in Kosovo consisted of by and large?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you something with respect to the entire operation, from the first day to your last day in Kosovo. According to you and the assessment of your comrades from the unit, did you perform that assignment well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now was there any kind of jeopardy involved over the civilian population exerted by the police, any violence at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you were in Kosovo, did you hear of any violence of the police against the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now let's move to the next time you went to Kosovo. And this took place between March and the second half of August 1998. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. You mean all the five assignments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all your assignments. After that, you were deployed and took control of the village of Gornji Streoci, Donji Streoci and you enabled communication along those lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No, we didn't take control of the villages. We ensured free communication and had checkpoints in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The point of my question was that you enabled communication to take place and that you held checkpoints along the communication lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, these villages, were they at some point in time in the hands of the terrorists who made it impossible for normal communication to be established and the normal use of those roads and communication lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. We were constantly under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were deployed at that time, together with your fellow policemen, to free the road passage from Decani to Pec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this road running from Pec to Decani, is that one of the main communication lines or main roads in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was an operation in which large KLA forces, terrorist forces of the KLA were engaged to cut off and close off an important communication line of that type?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were successful in opening up those lines of communication and life was deblocked in that part of Metohija which had otherwise been blocked with the blocking of the roads; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me this: When I say "you," I'm not referring to you personally. I'm thinking of the police force and the units you took part in. Did you, in that sense, on that occasion do anything whatsoever which in your opinion could have been a crime in professionally carrying out your legal assignment? Did you do that exclusively in the struggle against terrorism? Perhaps those were two questions in one, but I hope you understand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I just conducted my professional duties in conformity with the law, pursuant to the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no violence against the civilians, and you are not aware of any kind of crimes perpetrated against the civilians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, you describe an attempt on the part of your unit to attack Jablanica, which was being held by the KLA terrorists, but that you were not successful, that it was an abortive attempt because the terrorists had, as far as I'm able to learn, about 1.000 men in each shift there, up there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you went to Kosovo again the next time, your assignment was to deblock the entire length of road at the junction between Prilep and Junik, those crossroads, and the road leading to the village of Baboloc; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. That crossroads was the most threatened juncture along the whole road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is it true that that road was being held and blocked by the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. And six or seven times, at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had to deblock the road several times. And what you did was, in fact, a reaction to the fact that the roads had been blocked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you describe the operations that took place at the end of 1998, was the object and purpose of those operations the taking over of Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In describing the operations that took place at the end of 1998, the purpose and object of those operations was to take hold of Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Not in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah. I see in 1999. Now, is it true that Malisevo was to -- should have been taken control of because the terrorists were coming precisely from that area? And also in Malisevo they had their stronghold and base; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You personally took part in those operations, didn't you? Because I see that you describe the operation that took place to take control in the Kraljani area. Is it true that this was an operation undertaken because the Albanian terrorists had taken control of the television and communication relay station, and after that, they knocked it down, they knocked the relay station down. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: That wasn't at Kraljani. The TV repetitive station was at Budakovo in Suva Reka. And that's where they took control of it, and this took place at the beginning of May 1999, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in that operation, in the operation that had as its goal to drive them out of the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To push them away from that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the main reason for the operation taking control of the area in which these relay stations and repetitive stations were located -- repeater locations were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, at the time, you were helping the Nis special units because there were casualties in that particular unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the entire road from Suva Reka to Pristina was cut off. It had been cut off by the terrorists. And your task was, as far as I understand it, was exclusively to push them away from that road so that you could take control of the area. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me this: In view of the flow of that operation, was there any violence against civilians during that operation? That is to say on the part of our police force.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you go on to explain the operations undertaken at Mala Krusa, and I'm going to ask you several questions in that regard because you took part in the operation and the other side, the opposing side, is maintaining that the participants in Mala Krusa perpetrated war crimes. So here goes: Is it true that the plan of that operation was to push the terrorists back towards Malisevo where their headquarters and stronghold were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we hear mentioned daily here of some kind of cleansing, tell me, is it true that when the term "cleansing" or "mop-up" is mentioned and when a mop-up operation is mentioned that that implies and always means, without exception, repelling the terrorist KLA organisation? Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it never meant or implied anything that would jeopardise the security and safety of the civilians, the citizens themselves; right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: That's right. No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as you were a member of the PJP yourself, do you happen to know -- or, rather, did you have that kind of practice? Was it customary for the police to have an order not to open fire, even against the KLA, if this could jeopardise and threaten the lives of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, we did have orders of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there incidents that you are aware of where groups of civilians included members of the KLA who were easily identifiable because they would take off the upper parts of their uniform, and still the police did not take action even against them in order not to hurt the civilians? Do you know of any examples of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of this operation regarding Malisevo and repelling them towards Malisevo, I understood you as saying this morning when you were giving us your explanations that it was a part of a larger operation intended to diminish the territory controlled by the KLA in order to prevent or minimise the possible landing ground for the NATO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in a broader sense, this operation was intended to establish by all means control over the territory and not leave any part of the territory open to NATO attack and landing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. But also to repel them from the roads which was also -- from the roads which were blocked by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to ask you now in general terms about the relationship or, rather, the attitude of the police towards the civilians, the way they treated the civilians. Is it true that apart from repelling and neutralising the KLA or - in other words, your anti-terrorist actions - your next assignment was to collect the civilian population and extract it from the zone of combat operations for their own security? Is that so? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. That was always our objective in all operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, every time the police carried out an operation against the KLA in any area, there were always civilians involved and it was always necessary to extract them from the combat zone to protect them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this part of your activity was exclusively geared at protecting civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you - and when I say "you," I mean not you personally but the police - never expelled or took civilians outside of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, none of the men from my company did anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of anyone from the police who expelled or took people away from their home in order to drive them out of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No, I don't. And I had no contact with anyone outside the 23rd detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the KLA very often infiltrated groups of civilians who were pulled out of combat zones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. They did that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And more specifically, as far as I understood, you had orders to keep local police posted on the roads to prevent infiltration of KLA among the civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it primarily the task of the local MUP to take care of the civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after civilians were taken out of the zone of operations, there were instances when KLA infiltrated groups of civilians and, together with them, moved towards Albania and Macedonia? Do you know of any instances of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, when you describe the operation in Krusa, you didn't use any heavy weaponry, mortars, artillery or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: We didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding command, you were a corporal in a company. Is it customary to effect command within a company in direct contact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking this question because the opposite side had asked you if you had received any written orders. Would it be normal within one company which sticks together for anyone to issue written orders? Has that ever been the practice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you had appropriate training, do you know that this is the practice in any unit of the police or the army as far as communications within the company are concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had either live communication or through police radio; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what I can see, and I don't know if my conclusions are correct, your contacts, that is contacts of the police with superiors in the army of Yugoslavia, your impressions from the ground were that there was no relationship of hierarchy between the MUP and the army. Each had their own command.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: That is correct. They only interacted with us, and they had their own command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have explained something about this Velika Krusa operation. Is that true, that it was a stronghold of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. They had cut off the road, as we said, from Djakovica to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your view, was it a difficult operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Compared to the other operations, it was of medium difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Earlier today, in response to questions in chief, you said that the official assessment - by your superiors, I suppose - was that there were about 10.000 KLA members there and that amongst yourselves you privately believed that there were less of them, about 5.000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, but these assessments related to the entire territory, the broader operation. We believed, that's true, that there were less. But that was our individual opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it was your opinion there were 5.000 of them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the purpose of the operation was to push them back to the north; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They asked you earlier today whether some sort of alternative road was left to them which they could use for escape. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain whether that was done on all occasions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Every time we carried out such an action, beginning with 1998, an alternative route was always left for channeling both the terrorist organisation but also for extracting the refugees and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the MUP's assignment was to push back the terrorists towards the north, and that was one of the activities of your own unit; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was also your objective to establish communications in general, to normalise life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that before this operation, civilians had been displaced, but I understood you to mean that civilians had been displaced or moved out only for their protection.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. It was our objective precisely to move the civilian population out of the zone of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The civilians were not moved out in order to displace them or drive them out, just in order to take them out of the zone of combat operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to your own assessment, they needed to be protected precisely because they would have been in the danger of finding themselves in crossfire between the KLA on the one hand and the MUP and the army on the other side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us dwell on this issue for a while. Mop-up operations, when we use this term, that implies solely neutralising the KLA, and by no means does it mean expelling civilians from a certain segment of the territory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It implies only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that any member of the police ever drove civilians out within the framework of your testimony, what you have seen yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I never saw anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you comment upon or at least did you have any knowledge about the influence on the movement of civilians out of Kosovo of the fact that the KLA infiltrated groups of civilians and sometimes moved together with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: It may have crossed my mind, but I'm not sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the so-called forced displacements of civilians from certain territories is something you heard only from Albanians? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but they told all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke specifically about an incident which, as I noted down during your examination-in-chief, took place in the morning of the 23rd of March where several men were captured. Six men, more specifically, and all were members of the KLA. Was it visible and completely obvious that they were KLA members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. All of them had emblems and insignia of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see the arrest itself; you only saw them when they were already brought and captured.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they had only one rifle of Chinese production. Did you see that when they were brought or does it mean that all of them had only one rifle between them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I can't say exactly because I didn't see the arrest. I only know that one of them had a weapon. I don't know if the rest had weapons and had thrown them away before being brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was usual practice that when they were arrested they would throw away all their weapons into nearby bushes, shrubbery, wherever, before they would surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood you to say that they never entered your headquarters. Instead, members of your unit handed them over to a group of local policemen who took them away to a house near a river. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Although not near a river but 30 metres away from our position, towards the river as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any of those local policemen who took them over -- how many were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in your area, there were only three policemen from the local MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: They changed all the time. To the right of us, at an elevation, they had their own position which they held. Then they took turns. And there was always somebody from the local police at the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the intersection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it their job to guard this intersection or to hold an observation point or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: They had their own security checkpoint there, as in all other settlements behind the lines, towards which we would send men, women, and children for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You heard somebody shooting. Did you hear the shooting inside the house where they took those six men or did you simply see -- sorry, hear shooting nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I saw with my own eyes where they were taken, but I didn't hear shooting from that house, only from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I noted this down correctly because the opposite side had asked you when you went to that house. I understood you as saying that it might have been the following day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you went to that house the following day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I can't say precisely whether it was on the same or on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of that house, was there any local police at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No. There was no one either in the vicinity of the house or at the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you see when you entered the house? You said you saw several dead bodies. How many were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I didn't count.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you assert that it was there that the captives had been killed? Were you able to recognise or identify those same people that you had seen the previous day or earlier the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: I didn't look long enough to be able to say with certainty that those were the same men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were also asked about the care you took of the family of this local Albanian man you mentioned. You had your doubts as to the intentions of the local police. You thought that they might hurt them, and so you protected them. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Not exactly. Our vehicles were sheltered in their yard, and that's the reason why we were staying with them. They had a yard large enough to hide the vehicles so as not to be visible from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your explanation, since NATO was flying overhead, you were trying to preserve your combat vehicles. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of your unit towards those people? How did you treat them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: We treated them completely normally. We knocked on their door and explained the situation, and they allowed us to put our vehicles in their yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you asked them permission to use their yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't force the gates? You didn't mistreat them in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please describe this event. What was it like when this local policeman came and talked to them in the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Since they were at a distance from us, about 20 metres at that intersection, they came to see us and asked if there was anyone inside that house. I said no, there wasn't. The man didn't believe me and wanted to go inside himself and have a look. I didn't let him go on his own. I went with him and took him around all of the six houses, each of which was inhabited by one family. With all the men, all the Albanian men, he talked in Albanian and I could see from their eyes that he was threatening them. He also asked me personally to hand over to him all the Albanian men, which I refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, he left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes. We had a verbal duel, and after that, he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when that man came, there were three in total.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25
utterances.text: Yes -- or, rather, no. Two of them came to see us, and one of them wanted to go inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
